The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(v_p(n)\) be the exponent of prime \(p\) in \(n\).

For a move replacing \(a,b\) by \(\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\), the pair of exponents \(v_p(a),v_p(b)\) is replaced by \(\min(v_p(a),v_p(b)),\max(v_p(a),v_p(b))\). Thus for every prime \(p\), the multiset of the 2100 exponents \(v_p\) is invariant.

When Mark stops, every possible move leaves the board unchanged. For a pair \(x,y\), \(\{\gcd(x,y),\operatorname{lcm}(x,y)\}=\{x,y\}\) iff one of \(x,y\) divides the other. Therefore the final numbers form a divisibility chain.

Order the final numbers as
\[
x_1\mid x_2\mid \cdots \mid x_{2100}.
\]
For each prime \(p\), the exponents \(v_p(x_1),v_p(x_2),\dots,v_p(x_{2100})\) are nondecreasing, and their multiset is the same as the multiset of \(v_p(1),v_p(2),\dots,v_p(2100)\). Hence \(v_p(x_i)\) is the \(i\)-th smallest \(p\)-exponent among the original numbers.

We need \(i=2026\). For a prime \(p\), the number of original \(n\le 2100\) with \(v_p(n)\ge k\) is
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^k}\right\rfloor.
\]
The 2026th smallest exponent is at least \(k\) iff at least
\[
2100-2026+1=75
\]
numbers have exponent at least \(k\). So we need the largest \(k\) such that
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^k}\right\rfloor\ge 75.
\]
Since \(2100=75\cdot 28\), this is equivalent to
\[
p^k\le 28.
\]

Thus the exponents in the 2026th smallest final number are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p & \max\{k:p^k\le 28\}\\ \hline
2 & 4\\
3 & 3\\
5 & 2\\
7,11,13,17,19,23 & 1\\
\text{other primes} & 0
\end{array}
\]

So the 2026th smallest number is
\[
2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

Its number of positive divisors is
\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2^6
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
